newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CAR UNION UNABLE TO MEET ON PM ON TARIFFS
The main car industry union says it believes it has enough support in the Senate to stop car industry tariffs being cut further.
Cabinet has met today to consider its response to a Productivity Commission report which is understood to propose further tariff cuts to five percent by the year 2005.
The car industry says tariffs should be frozen at 15 per cent until 2006.
Manufacturing Workers' Union secretary, Doug Cameron, says it's clear the Government wants to continue tariff reductions, but Australia can't afford to lose any more jobs.
He says only the Prime Minister and other Government MPs did not go out of their way to meet with a delegation of workers in Canberra today.
TRADE DIALOGUE LAUNCHED BETWEEN TWO REGIONS
Australia's Trade Minister, Tim fischer says a new strategic dialogue between two important regions has been launched following a meeting between Australia, New Zealand and South American nations.
Mr Fischer met with his counterparts from four members of South America's common market, known as Mercosur, and New Zealand in Rio De Janerio to discuss strengthening trade and investment links.
He says there was a positive reaction from the Ministers to a proposal to examine expanding air links to improve tourism flows.
Mr Fischer says the meeting also agreed to begin work on an inter-regional agreement on investment.
BUSINESS OPTIMISM NOT REACHING AUSSIE EXECUTIVES
An economic consultant says the legacy of last year's tough Federal budget is holding back growth.

Duncan Ironmonger was commenting on a survey which found 13 percent of Australian firms hope to take on more staff in the June quarter, compared to about 30 per cent in the United States and New Zealand.
The survey by Dun and Bradstreet found 44 per cent of firms in Australia expect increased sales in the June quarter, compared to 63 percent in both the US and New Zealand.
Mr Ironmonger says he's not sure Australia will reach the growth heights that are currently being experienced in North America, New Zealand and Britain.
The survey of ten-thousand executives in 15 countries, found one of the biggest quarterly improvements in expectations, in nine years.
GOVT SAYS OVERSEAS PHONE CHARGES CAN IMPROVE
The Federal Government says there's still dramatic room for improvement in overseas phone call charges, following the revelation consumers are being charged inflated prices.
The Productivity Commission has found the cost of overseas calls is on average five times the cost Telstra and Optus face in providing international services.
Communications Minister Richard Alston says overseas call charges should fall once the telecommunications market is fully deregulated next month.
Senator Alston says consumers are currently getting a raw deal because of the lack of full blooded competition.
PM PRAISES POLICE
The Prime Minister has praised Australia's police officers, at a launch of a three-year national campaign to tackle violence and crime in communities.
The 13-million dollar campaign will target priority areas including residential burglary, fear of violence and crime, domestic violence and preventing juvenile crime.
The best methods will be assessed and tested in the community to ensure they work, and then made available for implementation across Australia.
Mr Howard says police officers are placed in despicable circumstances by law breakers.
He says they play a tremendous role in protecting the community, and have have copped a heavy battering through royal commissions and similar agencies in recent years.
"NOT ENOUGH BEING DONE" TO CONSERVE INLAND AUSTRALIA
A former head of the Department of Environment and Conservation says Australia's biggest environmental problem remains the degradation of inland areas.
Don McMichael was appointed to head the department when it was set up by the Whitlam Government in 1973.
On World Environment Day, Mr McMichael says not enough is being done to repair the damage grazing, salination and tree removal has caused.
While he says Australia's record when compared with other countries is relatively good, Mr McMichael says there is no reason it cannot be improved.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
